power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Eating disorders are serious psychological concerns associated with high levels of physical and psychological comorbidity and elevated premature mortality rates.
Despite the severity of these disorders, gaps in clinical care exist and most individuals with eating disorders either do not receive or do not benefit from existing evidence-based treatments.

There has been a growing movement to incorporate neuroscience-informed targets into eating disorder treatment; however, to date psychoeducation for eating disorders remains narrowly focused on eating-and weight-related behaviors and less directed towards their underlying mechanisms.

Yet, neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) can provide vital insights into diagnostic distinctions, patterns of psychiatric comorbidity, risk and maintenance mechanisms, brain-body relations, prognostic course, and therapeutic targets for eating disorders.

Further, knowledge of neuroscience can assist in designing the delivery of psychoeducation with the neurobiology of eating disorders in mind by tailoring content to consider the impact of personality and illness stage on the learning process.

In this chapter, we highlight the promise of NIPE for eating disorders, provide a case example of NIPE for eating disorders delivered in a clinical setting, and discuss future directions for research in this area.

Ultimately, NIPE can be used to bridge the gap between research knowledge and clinical care in eating disorders, thereby enhancing patient selfefficacy, dispelling misconceptions about eating disorders, and enhancing the accessibility of the science for individuals with these serious, yet undertreated disorders.

text.text: Several evidence-based treatments have been developed to address eating disorders.

text.text: While the current PE integrated into treatment helps patients, families, and clinicians understand the medical and psychological consequences of disordered eating, the lack of widespread neuroscience-based PE leaves many patients unaware of how brain processes contribute to their behaviors.
Most of this knowledge remains in academic journals instead of being translated into tools that connect neuroscience with lived NIPE for Eating Disorders 4 experience.
Neuroscience-informed PE (NIPE) offers a way to close that gap.
As the field increasingly recognizes eating disorders as neurobiologically-rooted conditions (Steinglass et al., 2019), NIPE provides a structure for bringing that understanding into treatment.

This chapter outlines a proposed structured model of NIPE for eating disorders in order to translate the science of the brain into the language of recovery.

The goal of integrating NIPE into eating disorder treatment is to offer patients a clearer picture of how brain processes contribute to the behaviors they engage in and how shifting brain function may also lead to symptom change.

Sharing this information can reduce self-blame (Lee et al., 2016), highlighting the role that underlying and typically invisible neural processes have in shaping emotions and behaviors that emerge over the course of the illness.

Diagnostic similarities and differences across eating disorder diagnoses: Certain patterns of brain activity have been demonstrated to be common across diagnoses.
For instance, there is evidence of hyper-sensitivity to threat and punishment that manifests across eating disorders (Harrison et al., 2010).

text.text: Potential shifts in neurobiological maintenance mechanisms over time: Emerging work suggests that the neurobiological and cognitive processes that maintain eating disorder symptoms in earlier stages of the disorder may differ from those that occur later in illness.

For instance, there are theories suggesting that binge eating behaviors in BN and BED and weight-loss behaviors in AN are goal-directed in early stages of illness, driven by activation of reward-circuitry (e.g. ventral striatum) upon receipt of food consumption or weight loss (and associated positive social feedback), respectively (Bodell & Racine, 2023; Steinglass & Walsh, 2006).

text.text: However, over time, binge eating and/or weight-loss behaviors may become overtrained, automatic, or driven by craving, despite no longer being associated with pleasurable outcomes.

text.text: Finally, eating disorder symptoms may play a role in fundamentally disrupting neurodevelopmental processes.

Emerging psychotherapy interventions for neurobiological targets: Although there is limited research about neurocognitive predictors of response to eating disorder treatment the emerging evidence linking neurocognitive processes to eating disorder treatment outcomes highlights the need for interventions to target such processes.

In recent years, a number of psychological and behavioral treatments for eating disorders, such as Relapse Prevention and Changing Habits (REACH+) (Steinglass et al., 2022), Temperament Based Treatment (Kaye et al., 2015), and Positive Affect Treatment (Haynos et al., 2024a), have been developed to target neurobiological mechanisms that may encourage or maintain eating pathology.

text.text: Incorporating information on varied biological interventions targeting neurobiological processes within NIPE could expand an awareness of novel avenues for eating disorder treatment and highlight the ability to manipulate neural disturbances perpetuating symptoms, further enhancing hope for pathways to recovery.

Balancing neurobiological explanations with personal agency: While neurobiological explanations for eating disorder behaviors may help reduce self-blame, NIPE should be presented in a way that emphasizes malleability rather than inevitability or permanence.

Pairing NIPE with information about neuroplasticity and reinforcing personal agency may help emphasize that neurobiological processes can change over the course of recovery and that individuals retain an active role in this process.
Together, these messages may promote optimism, self-efficacy, and hope for recovery (Farrell et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Together, these messages may promote optimism, self-efficacy, and hope for recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Farrell et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, discussions of neuroplasticity should be carefully framed to avoid implying that recovery depends on the complete normalization of a particular neural circuit or that such normalization is necessary for meaningful improvement.

Overall, neurobiological concepts should complement broader messages of agency, flexibility, and hope, allowing clinicians to incorporate neuroscience into care without overwhelming patients with an overly biologically-focused understanding of their disorder.
It is important to carefully consider how NIPE content is delivered to patients with eating disorders to ensure they gain the maximum benefit.
Given the medical and psychological sequelae in these disorders, a patient's current medical and psychiatric state should be taken into account before presenting this information.
Factors such as nutritional or illness status, temperament, mood, developmental stage, and past treatment experiences are especially important to consider.
Additionally, sociocultural factors should be considered when delivering NIPE, as eating disorders can present and be experienced differently across cultural and demographic groups.
Failure to adapt NIPE to these factors could make it harder for patients to meaningfully engage with and fully understand NIPE material.

Consideration of nutritional impairments and/or illness state: As mentioned, there are well documented impacts of acute and prolonged starvation on a range of cognitive abilities, including attention, executive functioning, and memory (Stedal et al., 2021), and their related brain systems (Koithan et al., 2024).

text.text: Therefore, careful consideration of nutritional state is needed when delivering NIPE.
When possible, it is important to encourage clients to come to treatment sessions appropriately nourished in order to better comprehend and retain the information provided.

NIPE content on the effects of nutritional status on brain function may reinforce the importance of adequate nourishment while providing an explanation for any cognitive slowing and fatigue patients may be experiencing.
It also may be helpful for clinicians to have snack foods available for individuals who come to session under-nourished.
Further, given the impact of eating disorder behaviors on higher-order cognitive processes, it is essential to tailor NIPE to be easy to comprehend and retain.
Brief, simple, and clear language suitable for a lay audience is preferrable, whereas highly detailed or technical descriptions of neuroscience-grounded concepts are discouraged.
Concrete prompts or reminders (e.g., worksheets, web-based materials) may support individuals with eating disorders in remembering the specifics of NIPE messaging in their daily lives.
It may also be useful to share NIPE with close others (e.g., parents, partners) who are supporting the person with an eating disorder in order to provide another source of consistent PE messaging.
Further, careful consideration is needed to determine what NIPE is appropriate for which stage of illness.

For instance, it is suggested that most active cognitive interventions for underweight or otherwise malnourished individuals are best suited for after they have undergone nutritional rehabilitation and experience the cognitive benefits of adequate caloric intake (American Psychiatric Association, 2023).
Therefore, it is possible that more complex NIPE concepts may be best suited to later stages of the treatment or recovery process, or may warrant consistent repetition across stages of recovery.

text.text: Thus, encouraging patients to approach NIPE information from a place of curiosity and openness may decrease potential pressure to "learn perfectly," inhibiting self-criticism that may interfere with learning.

Some individuals with eating disorders, especially those with restrictive eating disorders, experience high levels of perfectionism, harm avoidance, and emotional over-control (Atiye et al., 2015; Lampard et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Some individuals with eating disorders, especially those with restrictive eating disorders, experience high levels of perfectionism, harm avoidance, and emotional over-control <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Atiye et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Lampard et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For such individuals, NIPE content explaining the neurobiological mechanisms underlying their behaviors may be helpful in reducing anxiety by providing a sense of clarity regarding their symptoms, treatment course, and long-term outcomes.
It may also be helpful when working with such individuals to deliver NIPE in a manner that is structured, predictable, and concrete.
If information is presented in a vague or abstract way, the ambiguity may be experienced as distressing, distracting from the main objectives of the content.

In contrast, other individuals with eating disorders, especially those with binge eating disorders, show a tendency towards emotional under-control, novelty-seeking, and impulsivity (Atiye et al., 2015; Hill, 2024).
text.formatted: In contrast, other individuals with eating disorders, especially those with binge eating disorders, show a tendency towards emotional under-control, novelty-seeking, and impulsivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Atiye et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Hill, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For such individuals, it may be important for material to be novel and attention-grabbing.
For instance, engaging online platforms or interactive groups in which patients can share their lived experience of NIPE may increase and maintain interest in its content.
NIPE explaining reward processes underlying impulsivity may help patients understand how the way information is presented can influence their processing.
This may clarify the structure of NIPE while helping patients tailor their environment and communication to support learning and understanding throughout recovery.

Consideration of mood state: Depression and anxiety commonly co-occur across the eating disorder spectrum (Hambleton et al., 2022), which may influence how some patients process, retain, and engage with new PE content.
text.formatted: Consideration of mood state: Depression and anxiety commonly co-occur across the eating disorder spectrum <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Hambleton et al., 2022)</ref>, which may influence how some patients process, retain, and engage with new PE content.

text.text: Common depressive features such as slowed processing (LeMoult & Gotlib, 2019), reduced motivation (Treadway et al., 2012), and difficulties with sustained attention (Keller et al., 2019) can make relevant or interesting material feel overwhelming or unimportant.

text.text: This may translate to patients seeming unengaged with NIPE content even if this is inconsistent with their internal beliefs.

Similarly, individuals with anxiety often experience executive functioning deficits (Nyberg et al., 2021), emotional dysregulation (Mennin et al., 2005), and repetitive negative thinking (Petwal et al., 2023) which may lead to heightened emotional reactivity to potentially threatening material such as learning about their neurobiological risk factors.

text.text: For this reason, it is important for clinicians to thoroughly assess a patient's current mental state before introducing NIPE to ensure they can engage effectively and that receiving novel information will not be emotionally overwhelming.
Presenting NIPE material during extreme mood disturbances should be avoided, as this may reduce overall comprehension and retention.

For patients with psychiatric comorbidities, NIPE content addressing the neurobiological similarities between their eating disorder and their cooccurring condition can help patients understand how comorbidity influences symptom presentation and treatment engagement.
This may be particularly valuable when symptoms or illness-related cognitions conflict with their internal motivation to recover.

Clinicians may find that using simplified explanations, brief handouts, or more interactive approaches, or taking brief breaks, may make dense information seem more manageable for patients that are experiencing cognitive and emotional overload.
Consideration of developmental stage: NIPE for adolescents with eating disorders should be designed and presented to align with their developmental needs.

Because adolescents often have a shorter illness duration (Miskovic-Wheatley et al., 2023), they may be less familiar with the mechanisms and factors underlying the development and maintenance of their disorder.
text.formatted: Because adolescents often have a shorter illness duration <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Miskovic-Wheatley et al., 2023)</ref>, they may be less familiar with the mechanisms and factors underlying the development and maintenance of their disorder.

text.text: Adolescents are also experiencing ongoing development of higher-order cognitive functions and, thus, executive functioning skills may not be fully developed (Sydnor et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Adolescents are also experiencing ongoing development of higher-order cognitive functions and, thus, executive functioning skills may not be fully developed <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">(Sydnor et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, NIPE may need to be presented in a simplified, but detailed manner, with key concepts broken down into smaller, more comprehensible subconcepts.

Accompanying NIPE with visual aids (e.g., model of the brain), interactive exercises, or peer discussions may increase understanding and engagement by leveraging the increased sensitive to novelty and social experiences characteristic of this time period (Crone & Dahl, 2012).
text.formatted: Accompanying NIPE with visual aids (e.g., model of the brain), interactive exercises, or peer discussions may increase understanding and engagement by leveraging the increased sensitive to novelty and social experiences characteristic of this time period <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Crone & Dahl, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Presenting complex material in an age-appropriate and accessible way may help adolescents understand challenging topics without feeling disinterested or overwhelmed.
It is also important to deliver NIPE to families alongside adolescents to ensure everyone is educated about the neural consequences of the disorder in the same way.
In fact, research has demonstrated that PE delivered to families can reduce family burden and foster more positive interactions between adolescents and their families (Uehara et al., 2001).
text.formatted: In fact, research has demonstrated that PE delivered to families can reduce family burden and foster more positive interactions between adolescents and their families <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">(Uehara et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: NIPE content emphasizing heightened neuroplasticity during adolescence may further instill hope among adolescents and their loved ones while motivating adolescents to make meaningful changes that can support lasting recovery into adulthood.

Emerging evidence also suggests that NIPE can foster parental understanding of both their child's symptoms and overall temperamental patterns in a way that recontextualizes and destigmatizes behaviors that are often distressing to family members (Stedal et al., 2023).

text.text: Consideration of past treatments: Eating disorders can be enduring conditions with high rates of relapse (Richard et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Consideration of past treatments: Eating disorders can be enduring conditions with high rates of relapse <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">(Richard et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, many individuals often cycle in and out of treatment, which may affect the way that they interact with NIPE material.
This offers an opportunity to deliver more specialized NIPE to individuals with a chronic course of illness who are already familiar with many foundational concepts from past treatment.
For these individuals, novel material that offers new neuroscience-based insights that reframe their previous knowledge, or correct misconceptions about the implicated neural systems, is crucial.
Yet, prior research as demonstrated that biological explanations for eating disorders can reduce optimism for the future unless the malleability of these factors is emphasized (Farrell et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Yet, prior research as demonstrated that biological explanations for eating disorders can reduce optimism for the future unless the malleability of these factors is emphasized <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Farrell et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: For individuals with longer courses of illness in particular it may be important to emphasize NIPE as offering novel pathways to recovery.

In contrast, for patients new to treatment, NIPE that assumes prior knowledge can be overwhelming and lead to disengagement or frustration, especially for individuals with heightened threat sensitivity (Harrison et al., 2010).
text.formatted: In contrast, for patients new to treatment, NIPE that assumes prior knowledge can be overwhelming and lead to disengagement or frustration, especially for individuals with heightened threat sensitivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Harrison et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: For these reasons, clinicians may opt to align specific NIPE content with a patient's current stage in recovery.
Consideration of cultural, socioeconomic, and demographic background: Eating disorders are often misconceived as conditions that primarily affect affluent, White, cisgender women.

However, growing evidence demonstrates that eating disorders affect individuals across diverse socioeconomic, gender, body-size, and racial and ethnic backgrounds (Burke et al., 2023; Gorrell & Murray, 2019; López-Gil et al., 2023; Parker & Harriger, 2020).

text.text: For patients with marginalized backgrounds, NIPE should reflect the experiences of minoritized populations, as explanations that do not resonate with a patient's lived experience may perpetuate harmful stereotypes and misconceptions about who can develop and experience an eating disorder.

Although the core content of NIPE may remain largely unchanged, tailoring its delivery to explicitly challenge stereotypical presentations of eating disorders and recognize cultural and socioeconomic barriers to nutrition and treatment may enhance its relevance and help reduce stigma (Husain et al., 2017; Shin, 2004).

text.text: NIPE for such populations may also benefit by emphasizing the noted NIPE for Eating Disorders 23 impact of stigma and discrimination on the functioning of many of the neural circuits implicated in eating pathology, highlighting ways in which external influences may impact neurobiological processes (Berger & Sarnyai, 2015).

text.text: Additionally, NIPE should account for the broad spectrum of eating disorder presentations and be adapted to the distinct experiences and needs of diverse patient populations.

For example, NIPE addressing disturbed interoception as a mechanism maintaining an eating disorder should be tailored differently for an adult with BED in a larger body, a male with AN, and an adolescent with sensory-based ARFID, with neuroscientific explanations adapted to reflect the distinct experiences associated with each presentation.
Below, we provide a case example demonstrating the implementation of NIPE into medical visits and psychological treatment.
At presentation to outpatient treatment, Lorraine was a 34-year-old White, bisexual, cisgender woman who lived with her partner in the Midwest and worked full-time as an elementary school teacher.
Lorraine shared that she had struggled with her eating patterns and body image since she was 16 years old.
She stated that she had a long-standing history of depressive symptoms that started in childhood, but escalated during adolescence.

During that time, she had incidentally attempted a popular diet plan alongside some friends and had been pleasantly surprised by how the resulting weight loss helped to alleviate her momentary feelings of low mood.
She found that, although her friends ultimately abandoned the diet fad, she felt increasingly "addicted" to weight loss, pursuing it until she reached an underweight state.

Since then, her symptoms had fluctuated over time, such that she experienced some periods of heightened restriction accompanied by low weight, as well as other periods in which she was able to eat relatively normally and maintain a healthier weight.
More recently, eating disorder symptoms had escalated following a number of stressors, including a job loss and ongoing conflict with her partner.
However, she was not aware of the severity of her recent eating concerns until she was referred to a partial hospitalization program (PHP) by her primary care physician.

At admission to the PHP, her symptoms were consistent with AN, restricting subtype, with a BMI of 16.4 kg/m 2 , severe food restriction, excessive exercise patterns, strict dietary rules, and shape and weight concerns.
Lorraine was discharged from the PHP at a BMI of 20.5 kg/m 2.
Although her overall caloric intake increased following PHP, she continued to endorse strict dietary rules, as well as heightened concerns about shape and weight after discharge.
She often experienced symptoms of depression and anxiety related to her eating disorder symptoms and worried she would not be able to achieve full recovery.

She described feeling shame that she continued to struggle with eating disorder symptoms after so many years, especially because she knew that these behaviors put a strain on her relationship with her partner.

NIPE was incorporated into the outpatient treatment for Lorraine to help her better understand how her symptoms had developed and been maintained over time in a way that could reduce her self-blame related to her ongoing struggles.
Further, NIPE was used to highlight directions for intervention and to enhance a sense of hope that the symptoms that she was experiencing could be reduced by "retraining" her brain.

Given Lorraine's tendency towards a concrete and detail-oriented cognitive style, the therapist made sure to break NIPE concepts into small, manageable bits of information, supported by concrete examples and written materials.

Additionally, the therapist took into consideration Lorraine's nutritional state and mood when presenting NIPE material, with more novel and complex information being presented at times when Lorraine arrived more adequately nourished and less acutely distressed.

The therapist also NIPE for Eating Disorders 25 encouraged Lorraine to share the NIPE discussed in treatment with her partner in order to support their understanding of the factors leading to Lorraine's struggles with eating.

At the beginning of treatment, the therapist began by describing how Lorraine's eating disorder symptoms may have originally developed through a combination of her neurocognitive tendencies interacting with the unique brain development processes occurring in adolescence.
Specifically, the therapist highlighted that adolescence is a period in which reward circuitry is sensitized and executive functioning skills and their underlying circuits are still being developed.

Therefore, Lorraine may have been especially sensitive to the reward of weight loss, especially when it was paired with social connection and praise, and also developmentally limited in her ability to comprehend the long-term consequences of her eating disorder symptoms and to shift her behavior accordingly.

This process may have interacted with Lorraine's general tendency towards cognitive rigidity and perseverance, which may have explained why she had persisted in restrictive eating even once her friends had stopped.

This information was helpful in combating the messaging that Lorraine had received from friends and family members when she was younger that had indicated that her behaviors were "selfish" or "manipulative."

By highlighting that these behaviors were direct results of normative brain processes gone awry, and that her mental tendencies contributing to symptom maintenance (e.g., cognitive persistence) were not inherently bad and had been helpful in other contexts (e.g., academic success), Lorraine was able to experience diminished self-blame.

When introducing NIPE into Lorraine's understanding of the maintenance of her disorder, the therapist highlighted that individuals with restrictive eating disorders demonstrate neurobiological patterns characterized by: 1) increased threat detection in response to eating-and body-related stimuli; 2) heightened reward responsivity to weight-loss cues; 3) diminished NIPE for Eating Disorders 26 reward responsivity to other pleasant stimuli; 4) over-engagement of cognitive control circuitry; and 5) limited ability to understand and respond to interoceptive signals.
As such, her brain was primed to look to eating disorder symptoms as a solution to reduce her pervasive experience of aversive reactivity and anhedonia.
Additionally, Lorraine's neurobiological tendencies may have made it easier for her to engage her cognitive control circuitry than to understand her bodily experiences and needs.

Lorraine reported this explanation aligned with her experience, such that she often found that her eating disorder symptoms became the "solution" to any of her problems, whether it be a distressing interaction with her partner or feeling of being out of control of her work situation.

She also reported continuing to struggle with interpreting bodily cues for hunger following weight restoration, regularly doubting her internal sensations and opting to suppress these feelings instead.

The therapist also introduced the concept that, over time, the way in which her eating disorder symptoms interacted with her brain may have shifted, such that her behavior came under the control of more automatic areas of the brain associated with wanting or striving, rather than acute pleasure.

Lorraine indicated that this was one of the most frustrating aspects of her experience -she desperately wanted to change her eating disorder behaviors, but found it had become increasingly difficult to do so.
Once Lorraine had learned about how neural processes contributed to her disorder, her therapist shifted towards utilizing NIPE technique to motivate ongoing recovery actions.

First, the therapist highlighted that the process of nutritional rehabilitation and weight restoration alone had already gone a long way towards correcting some of the neurobiological disturbances that had kept her stuck.
Lorraine acknowledged that, since weight restoration, she had been less emotionally reactive, more positively engaged in her life, and less preoccupied with eating disorder thoughts.

The therapist emphasized the importance of Lorraine continuing to maintain NIPE for Eating Disorders 27 weight and a regular pattern of eating in order to foster longer-term restoration of neurocognitive functioning.

Second, the therapist introduced the concept of neuroplasticity, explaining that, although Lorraine's brain had developed certain patterns of responding to eating disorder cues and perceived threats and rewards more generally, these could be altered through targeted interventions.
The end result would be the development of new neural pathways to support more effective patterns of behavior.

The therapist stated that targeting established neurocognitive eating disorder mechanisms had the potential to not only ease Lorraine's eating disorder symptoms, but also many of her accompanying affective symptoms.
Lastly, Lorraine's therapist described the existing and emerging psychological and biological treatments designed with these targets in mind.

This discussion provided Lorraine with a newfound sense of hope that her biological-rooted drive towards restrictive eating and weight loss was modifiable and that options existed for targeting these patterns in treatment.

This case example briefly illustrates how NIPE can be incorporated into everyday conversations with patients who struggle to understand the factors driving their behaviors or who frequently engage in self-blame, holding themselves responsible for their disorder.

Additionally, the emphasis of neural plasticity and the reversibility of these neural dysfunctions can help patients recognize that recovery is achievable and that small, gradual steps can foster lasting neural rehabilitation.

Although this example specifically focuses on the neural mechanisms underlying restrictive eating in AN, the aim is to demonstrate how clinicians can translate complex neuroscience into a digestible and personalized format that patients can understand and share with others.
Lorraine's case can be adapted to reflect the specific eating disorder diagnosis she experiences.

For example, if Lorraine instead had a diagnosis of BED and presented with NIPE for Eating Disorders 28 emotion dysregulation and impulsivity, the therapist might instead work to ensure NIPE was highly engaging through heightened use of interactive exercises and real-world practice and place greater emphasis on reward circuitry and the reinforcing effects of binge eating, rather than on weight loss.

NIPE could focus on how binge eating frequently develops during a developmental period where adolescent brains are primed to respond to primary rewards, such as food, and that, over time, binge eating becomes an overlearned strategy for regulating negative affect during stressful situations or a craving-driven process.

Alternatively, if Lorraine had ARFID and presented with strong aversions to particular food textures, tastes, or smells, the therapist might place less emphasis on neurobiological mechanisms underlying weight or shape.

Instead, NIPE could be tailored to explain how differences in sensory processing and interoceptive awareness can contribute to food avoidance, emphasizing that this avoidance reflects underlying neurobiological processes rather than intentional refusal or lack of motivation to eat.

Thus, while the core principles of NIPE can be applied transdiagnostically, the content and emphasis of NIPE can be adapted to the distinct maintaining mechanisms and symptom presentations associated with each disorder.

As with all NIPE content, explanations should be tailored to the individual patient and informed by their unique experiences.

NIPE occupies a growing intersection between research, clinical practice, and lived experience and offers a shared language for understanding recovery in ways that emphasized the role of relevant neurobiological processes.
However, systematic effort is required to integrate NIPE for Eating Disorders 29 NIPE in a meaningful and practical way.
The next phase of work should focus on testing, refining, and expanding NIPE to ensure it remains empirically grounded, clinically useful, and responsive to the people and systems it aims to serve.
We have outlined below several priorities for advancing this work.

Strengthening translation between neuroscience and clinical practice: Intentional translation of neuroscience into clinical practice is a vital in bridging the researchpractice gap (Hildebrandt & Goldschmidt, 2024).
text.formatted: Strengthening translation between neuroscience and clinical practice: Intentional translation of neuroscience into clinical practice is a vital in bridging the researchpractice gap <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Hildebrandt & Goldschmidt, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Clinicians need accessible ways to interpret and apply neuroscientific findings, while researchers need feedback from those working directly with patients to ensure their work reflects real world needs.

Thus, stronger efforts are needed to bridge the bench-to-bedside divide by considering the clinical consequences of neuroscience research, as well as the clinical findings that may shape an understanding of neurobiological targets.
There is growing recognition of the need to involve individuals with lived experiences of mental illness, including eating disorders, into research (Schleider, 2023).
text.formatted: There is growing recognition of the need to involve individuals with lived experiences of mental illness, including eating disorders, into research <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">(Schleider, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, NIPE should be shaped collaboratively with individuals who have experienced eating disorders, their families, and the practitioners (e.g., therapists, dieticians, medical providers) that work closest to them.

Co-designing materials helps ensure that neuroscientific concepts are accurately tailored to real-life experiences (Downs, 2024) and explained in ways that are understandable, relevant, and relatable.
text.formatted: Co-designing materials helps ensure that neuroscientific concepts are accurately tailored to real-life experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Downs, 2024)</ref> and explained in ways that are understandable, relevant, and relatable.

text.text: Their input can also guide how information is framed and delivered so it fits the realities of different recovery paths and care settings.
To move NIPE from concept to practice, its impact should be tested in eating disorder settings.
Directly testing NIPE will be critical to establishing its efficacy and advancing the integration of evidence-based neuroscience into eating disorder care.
Research must examine not only whether NIPE works, but when, for whom, and under what conditions.
These studies should account for factors such as illness stage, cognitive flexibility, and readiness for recovery while recognizing that PE may influence people differently across these contexts.
Evaluation should also include all intended audiences -patients, families, and clinicians -since each engages with NIPE in distinct ways that shape understanding and outcomes.

In addition to evaluating the benefits of NIPE, it will be important to evaluate potential pitfalls of such approaches (Angermeyer et al., 2013), as well as ways to mitigate any unintended harms of such explanations.

text.text: Understanding how to best teach NIPE to clients, support systems and practitioners:
Teaching neuroscience effectively is central to the impact of NIPE.
Future work should determine how to present complex brain concepts in ways that match people's cognitive and emotional capacities during recovery.

Consistent with the NIPE framework presented by Rezapour and colleagues (2026), it will be important to determine how to frame NIPE for families and clinicians in order to balance structure with empathy that can help turn neuroscience into care that builds understanding and connection.

text.text: Integrating emerging technologies to expand NIPE's reach and relevance: Emerging technologies offer promising ways to bring NIPE to life.

Interactive tools, virtual environments, and adaptive learning platforms can help visualize brain processes, tailor content to individual learning needs, and provide feedback that deepens understanding (Schleisman et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Interactive tools, virtual environments, and adaptive learning platforms can help visualize brain processes, tailor content to individual learning needs, and provide feedback that deepens understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Schleisman et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Used intentionally, these innovations can make complex brain-behavior concepts feel tangible and empowering, extending NIPE outside formal treatment settings and into the broader recovery landscape.
NIPE for eating disorders may be integrated into traditional or emerging treatment approaches to help patients understand how their brain and its processes influence their thoughts and behaviors.
Treatment for eating disorders often involves encouraging patients to adjust maladaptive cognitive and behavioral patterns.
Providing neuroscientific insight into the origins of these thought and behavior patterns and the potential neural gains associated with change may support sustained motivation in recovery.

Despite the growth of neuroscientific research on eating disorders (Steinglass et al., 2019), there remains a lack of consideration in the field on how to effectively educate patients about these findings.

text.text: NIPE can be used to bridge the gap between research knowledge and clinical care in order to bolster patient self-efficacy, dispel common misconceptions about eating disorders, and enhance the accessibility of the science behind behavior change for individuals with eating disorders.

NIPE about neural risk and resiliency factors can help patients recognize that certain neurobiological factors beyond their control may have made them more vulnerable to developing an eating disorder.
This information can also guide providers in recognizing the neurocognitive factors that may place individuals at risk of developing future eating pathology.

Although research on these factors remains an emerging area, clinicians can still discuss them with patients while explicitly distinguishing between what is currently known and what NIPE for Eating Disorders 13 remains under investigation.

Doing so may reinforce that our understanding of the brain's role in eating pathology continues to evolve, while also helping to bridge the researchpractice gap in both clinicians' and patients' understanding of eating disorders.
